newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai government applauded for seeking IMF help.
newsitem.headline: Thai government applauded for seeking IMF help.

text.p: Thailand has gained business and public support for its decision to seek financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to revive the troubled economy.
Thailand's worst economic crisis in several decades, which threatened to bankrupt its financial sector, forced its government and business community to swallow national pride and seek IMF help.
Analysts on Monday voiced approval of an austerity package being worked out by Thai and IMF officials, saying its long-term benefits justified the short-term economic pain.

"It is time for us to help by changing our lifestyle, by cutting back on our over-spending and excessive investment to concentrate on boosting efficiency," said Preecha Jarungidanan, director of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities Co Ltd.

Thai and IMF officials this week were putting the finishing touches on an economic package expected by the market to include a multi-billion dollar IMF standby credit, tough monetary and fiscal discipline and reform of debt-ridden financial and property sectors.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Monday he would seek cabinet approval of the IMF-backed package framework on Tuesday. Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said clearer details of the package would likely emerge by early next week.
The Japanese financial newspaper Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday the Japan Export-Import Bank and IMF planned to put together an $8 billion emergency loan package for Thailand.

Analysts traced the burst of the Thai economic bubble to a surge of foreign loans imported by the private sector during Thailand's boom years in the first half of the 1990s after the country lifted its foreign exchange controls.
They said about 43 percent of Thailand's $86 billion foreign debts were short-term private borrowing, with a substantial portion of it invested in its collapsed property industry.

Anaemic exports and a property sector crash in 1996 induced capital flight that put pressure on the baht, culminating in its de facto devaluation on July 2. The currency has since depreciated about 20 percent.

Analysts said mounting economic problems helped Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh as he sought to convince his five coalition partners of the need to accept the IMF package, expected to include hefty budget cuts for the 1997/1998 (October-September) fiscal year.
A senior finance ministry official said, however, that Thailand may negotiate for a budget cut smaller than one recommended by the IMF.
Thai media said the IMF had suggested that Thailand slash its 1997/98 fiscal budget by 100 billion baht ($3.2 billion).

"The more crucial issue is on which budgets to be cut, rather than by how much. The IMF would likely call for budget cuts that do not affect infrastructure projects but on things like arms acquisitions," said Preecha of Chao Phaya Finance.
"I think the overall package should be accepted as it would help rebuild confidence," he said.

Banks and finance companies, hurt by a severe liquidity crunch for more than a year, are also prepared to sacrifice by allowing greater foreign competition that would follow further financial liberalisation to be included in the reform package.
"It's better than the prospect of seeing us squeezed dry," said Som Jatusripitak, president of Siam City Bank Plc and former head of the Thai Bankers Association.
Analysts also expected the IMF to demand the government stop using taxpayers' money to bail out weak firms in the 91-company non-bank finance sector hit by mounting non-performing loans.
Most analysts agreed with an expected IMF proposal for Thailand to raise its value added tax (VAT) to 10 percent from the current seven percent.

"A 10 percent VAT is not that high. It should be raised to induce a change in wasteful consumption behaviour, especially luxury spending by the rich. The question is efforts should be made to spare hardship to be imposed on the poor," a university lecturer said.
